scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

Let me start by understanding the situation better. My brother is two years younger than me and has Asperger's. We've known about his diagnosis for years, but it's not something we talk about much in our family because he's embarrassed about it. Despite that, he's extremely smart, excels in math and physics, and is doing well in college. Lately, he's been really depressed, even to the point of attempting suicide a few months ago. He called me in a panic, and I took him to the hospital. After that, he went through outpatient treatment. Recently, a nurse asked me if my brother had ever been diagnosed with autism because she noticed some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today, but he's still denying that he has autism. He loves me a lot, and I love him just as much. We've always been close, and as we've gotten older, we've become more alike, which he really likes. I've tried talking to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed of it. I've mentioned that some people think famous figures like Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Asperger's, but that doesn't seem to help him. I'm considering telling him that I have Asperger's too, thinking that it might help him accept his diagnosis and not feel alone. But I'm wondering if that's a good idea or if I'd be being a jerk by lying to him for the rest of our lives. First, I need to understand why my brother is denying his diagnosis. Maybe he feels ashamed or doesn't want to be labeled. I can see how that would be tough, especially since he's so smart and successful in many areas. But his depression and the suicide attempt are serious issues that I need to take into account. If I lie to him about having Asperger's, what are the potential consequences? On one hand, it might make him feel less alone and more accepting of his diagnosis. On the other hand, lying could damage our trust and relationship. He might feel betrayed if he finds out I lied to him. I also need to consider whether there are other ways to help him without lying. Maybe I can find resources or support groups where he can connect with others who have Asperger's. Or perhaps I can encourage him to talk to a therapist who specializes in autism spectrum disorders. Another thing to think about is the impact of my actions on myself. If I lie to him, would I feel guilty or stressed about maintaining that lie? It might affect my mental health as well. I should also think about the long-term implications. If I lie now, what happens if he finds out later? How would that affect our relationship? It's possible that the short-term benefits of making him feel better might not outweigh the long-term damage to our trust. Maybe instead of lying, I can approach the conversation more gently. I can express my support and let him know that I'm here for him, regardless of his diagnosis. I can share positive stories about people with Asperger's who have achieved great things, but without lying about my own situation. I also need to respect his autonomy. He has the right to make his own decisions about how he identifies and what he shares about himself. My role is to support him, not to control his feelings or decisions. In summary, while my intention is to help my brother feel less alone and more accepting of his diagnosis, lying about having Asperger's myself might not be the best approach. It could lead to trust issues and might not address the root of his denial or depression. Instead, I should focus on providing him with genuine support, resources, and a safe space to talk about his feelings without judgment.
